In addition to these primary outcomes, several studies used disease-specific or function-specific instruments to assess multidimensional health status, including quality-of-life scales, functional mobility tests, lower-limb performance tests, walking capacity measures, body composition indicators, and cardiometabolic markers. These indicators provided a comprehensive framework for evaluating the effects of HBE on body composition, physical function, cardiometabolic health, and HRQoL in postmenopausal and older women.
Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for all 19 included trials. The judgments for individual trials are presented in Figure 2B, and the distribution of judgments across domains in Figure 2A.
Figure 2. (A) Risk-of-bias bar plot. The figure summarizes the proportion of judgments across RoB 2 domains. (B) Risk-of-bias traffic-light plot. The figure shows domain-level risk-of-bias judgments for each included randomized controlled trial.

Overall, four trials (21.1%) were judged to be at low risk of bias, 13 (68.4%) raised some concerns, and two (10.5%) were at high risk of bias.
Selection of the reported result was the most frequent source of concern: 11 trials (57.9%) raised some concerns and eight (42.1%) were judged to be at low risk. In most of these trials no trial protocol or prespecified statistical analysis plan was available, so it could not be verified that the reported results corresponded to a prespecified analysis. No trial was judged to be at high risk in this domain.
Bias arising from the randomization process was the next most frequent concern, with nine trials (47.4%) raising some concerns and one trial (5.3%) judged to be at high risk. In most of these trials the method used to generate the random sequence, or the method used to conceal the allocation, was not reported in sufficient detail.

Deviations from the intended interventions rarely raised concern: 17 trials (89.5%) were judged to be at low risk, one trial (5.3%) raised some concerns, and one trial (5.3%) was at high risk. Although blinding of participants and personnel is not feasible in exercise trials, most trials reported an analysis consistent with the intention-to-treat principle, whereas no information was available in the trial judged to be at high risk on whether an appropriate analysis had been used to estimate the effect of assignment to intervention.
Missing outcome data raised no concern in any trial (19 of 19, 100%), as attrition was low or was accounted for in the analysis.
Measurement of the outcome raised some concerns in two trials (10.5%), in which outcome assessors were not blinded, or the outcome was self-reported without further safeguards.

Because trials judged to raise some concerns account for a substantial share of the evidence for several outcomes, the certainty of the evidence was downgraded accordingly in the GRADE assessment (Supplementary Table S3).
Nineteen trials were included in the quantitative synthesis; 18 entered the main analysis, and the single trial with an active comparator is described separately. Home-based exercise was compared with an inactive control in 15 trials and with an attention control in three trials. All analyses used a random-effects model with the REML estimator for τ2 and the Hartung–Knapp adjustment, and prediction intervals are reported for outcomes with substantial heterogeneity. The overall results are summarized in Table 3.
Four trials (n = 197) reported BMI. Heterogeneity was low (I^2 = 0%), and the pooled mean difference indicated a significant reduction favoring home-based exercise (MD = −0.57 kg/m^2; 95% CI: −0.71 to −0.43; p < 0.001; Figure 3). Because a lower BMI is not universally beneficial, particularly among older women with frailty, this result is reported as a reduction in BMI rather than as an improvement.

Figure 3. Forest plot of body mass index (BMI). Effect sizes are expressed as mean differences (MDs) in change from baseline with 95% confidence intervals.
Four trials (n = 195) reported body fat percentage. The pooled effect did not reach statistical significance (MD = −0.31%; 95% CI: −0.65 to 0.03; I^2 = 0%; p = 0.06; Figure 4). The small number of contributing studies and differences in body composition assessment methods limit interpretation.
Figure 4. Forest plot of body fat percentage (BFP). Effect sizes are expressed as mean differences (MDs) in change from baseline with 95% confidence intervals.
Four trials (n = 261) reported the TUGT. Heterogeneity was substantial (I^2 = 83%), and the pooled effect did not reach statistical significance (MD = −0.64 s; 95% CI: −1.57 to 0.30; p = 0.12; Figure 5). The prediction interval (−2.69 to 1.42 s) crossed the null, indicating that a future trial could plausibly show no effect or a reversal.

Figure 5. Forest plot of the Timed Up-and-Go Test (TUGT). Effect sizes are expressed as mean differences (MDs) in change from baseline with 95% confidence intervals; the 95% prediction interval is also shown.
Four trials (n = 317) reported the 5 × STS. The pooled effect did not reach statistical significance (MD = −1.92 s; 95% CI: −4.36 to 0.52; I^2 = 43%; p = 0.09; Figure 6).
Figure 6. Forest plot of the five-times sit-to-stand test (5 × STS). Effect sizes are expressed as mean differences (MDs) in change from baseline with 95% confidence intervals.
Four trials (n = 226) assessed handgrip strength by dynamometry. The pooled effect did not reach statistical significance (MD = 1.43 kg; 95% CI: −1.02 to 3.88; I^2 = 43%; p = 0.16; Figure 7). Handgrip strength should be interpreted as one indicator of muscle function rather than as a comprehensive measure of upper-limb strength.

Figure 7. Forest plot of handgrip strength. Effect sizes are expressed as mean differences (MDs) in change from baseline with 95% confidence intervals.
Three trials (n = 133) reported the 6MWT, and all data were converted to meters. The pooled estimate is reported in Table 3 (MD = 35.16 m; 95% CI: −59.96 to 130.29; Figure 8) together with the individual trial estimates in Supplementary Table S2. It should be interpreted with caution: the contributing trials differed markedly in population and in the scale of change, heterogeneity was substantial (I^2 = 87%), and the prediction interval (−151.67 to 222.00) crossed the null.
Figure 8. Forest plot of the six-minute walk test (6MWT). Effect sizes are expressed as mean differences (MDs) in change from baseline with 95% confidence intervals; the 95% prediction interval is also shown.

Three trials (n = 232) reported serum triglyceride concentrations. The pooled effect did not reach statistical significance (MD = −8.96 mg/dL; 95% CI: −19.45 to 1.52; I^2 = 0%; p = 0.07; Figure 9).
Figure 9. Forest plot of serum triglycerides. Effect sizes are expressed as mean differences (MDs) in change from baseline with 95% confidence intervals.
SBP and DBP were each reported by two trials and were therefore not pooled. The individual estimates are presented in Supplementary Table S2. Neither outcome showed a significant between-group difference, and the confidence intervals were wide.
Ten trials (n = 463) assessed HRQoL using both generic (SF-36, EQ-5D, FACT-G) and disease-specific (MLHFQ, JOQOL, QUALEFFO-41, FACT-En, EORTC QLQ-C30, MENQOL) instruments; scores were direction-harmonized so that higher values indicate better HRQoL. The pooled effect favored home-based exercise (SMD = 0.51; 95% CI: 0.08 to 0.94; I^2 = 76%; p = 0.025; Figure 10), but the prediction interval (−0.75 to 1.78) crossed the null.

In subgroup analysis by instrument type, the effect was 0.35 (95% CI: −0.36 to 1.06) for generic instruments (k = 4) and 0.61 (95% CI: −0.13 to 1.35) for disease-specific instruments (k = 6), with no significant difference between subgroups (p = 0.48; Supplementary Figure 9).
Figure 10. Forest plot of health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Effect sizes are expressed as standardized mean differences (SMDs) in change from baseline with 95% confidence intervals; the 95% prediction interval is also shown.
Exploratory subgroup analyses were performed to examine potential sources of heterogeneity; all strata are reported in Supplementary Table S4, and the analysis for the HRQoL outcome that was judged interpretable is shown in Supplementary Figure 10. For HRQoL, subgroup analysis by comparator tier showed that the eight trials with inactive controls were considerably more homogeneous (I^2 = 16%) than the two trials with attention controls (I^2 = 71%), with pooled estimates of 0.29 (95% CI: 0.02 to 0.57) and 1.44 (95% CI: −4.67 to 7.56) respectively.

This indicates that much of the heterogeneity in this outcome arises from the two attention-controlled trials, and is consistent with the sensitivity analysis reported in Section 3.6.
Between-subgroup tests were also computed for instrument type, menopausal status ascertainment, comorbidity, session frequency and intervention duration, but the number of trials per stratum ranged from one to nine and these tests are not adjusted for the small number of trials; none of them is therefore interpreted, consistent with the guidance that a between-subgroup difference alone does not demonstrate effect modification. For the TUGT (k = 4) and the 6MWT (k = 3), subgroup analysis was not informative; the heterogeneity of these outcomes is instead reflected in their prediction intervals, which cross the null.

Because the risk of bias of the contributing trials should inform the interpretation of the pooled estimates, the analyses were also repeated with the two trials judged to be at high risk of bias overall removed. The BMI estimate was unchanged (MD = −0.57 kg/m^2; 95% CI: −0.71 to −0.43), and the HRQoL estimate remained significant and was slightly larger (SMD = 0.58; 95% CI: 0.12 to 1.04; I^2 = 76%; p = 0.019). The TUGT estimate moved toward the null and its heterogeneity resolved (k = 3; MD = −0.20 s; 95% CI: −0.71 to 0.32; I^2 = 0%), indicating that the heterogeneity of this outcome was attributable largely to that trial; body fat percentage was unchanged in direction and remained non-significant (k = 3; MD = −0.29%; 95% CI: −0.98 to 0.39). Restriction of the analyses to the four trials judged to be at low risk of bias was not estimable for any outcome.

Leave-one-out analyses showed that no single trial altered the pooled BMI estimate (Supplementary Figure 1; the corresponding analyses for the remaining outcomes are presented in Supplementary Figures 2–8). For HRQoL, the pooled estimate remained significant after excluding the two studies that reported only a single SF-36 domain (SMD = 0.57; 95% CI: 0.04 to 1.09; I^2 = 79%; p = 0.038; Supplementary Figure 11) and after restricting the analysis to trials with inactive comparators (k = 8) (SMD = 0.29; 95% CI: 0.02 to 0.57; I^2 = 16%; p = 0.040). It remained significant, with a wider confidence interval, after excluding the two trials judged to raise some concerns for outcome measurement (SMD = 0.60; 95% CI: 0.06 to 1.13; I^2 = 79%; p = 0.034), but was no longer significant after restricting to trials with documented menopausal status (grades A and B; k = 5) (SMD = 0.31; 95% CI: −0.05 to 0.66; I^2 = 0%; p = 0.072) and after excluding all grade C trials (k = 7) (SMD = 0.51; 95% CI: −0.11 to 1.12; p = 0.089). The HRQoL finding should therefore be interpreted as preliminary.

Publication bias was assessed for HRQoL, the only outcome approaching the minimum number of studies for a funnel plot. Visual inspection of the funnel plot (Figure 11) did not suggest marked asymmetry and Egger’s regression test was not statistically significant (p = 0.97); trim-and-fill added no studies. However, with only ten studies and substantial heterogeneity (I^2 = 76%), the power of this test is limited and publication bias cannot be excluded. Formal assessment was not possible for BMI, TUGT, 5 × STS, handgrip strength, body fat percentage, triglycerides, 6MWT, SBP or DBP because too few studies were available.
Figure 11. Funnel plot for publication bias assessment of health-related quality of life (HRQoL). The plot was used for visual inspection of publication bias for the HRQoL outcome.

Safety, adherence and feasibility were extracted from all included trials and are reported in Table 5. Eight trials explicitly reported no adverse events; two reported mild events, namely transient generalized soreness, bruising, and myalgia resolving within about 1.5 weeks; and one reported a fall resulting in a forearm fracture together with three cases of back pain during training that resolved on cessation, with no new vertebral fractures; the source report did not establish a causal attribution of these events to the exercise program. Eight trials did not report adverse events. Adherence ranged from 66 to 100% where reported; adherence data could not be retrieved in one trial because the application’s usage records were automatically deleted and home exercise logs had not been collected. This review did not directly evaluate feasibility, acceptability or implementation outcomes, and the included trials were not designed to assess them.

This systematic review and meta-analysis included 19 randomized controlled trials involving 1,128 postmenopausal and older women and evaluated the effects of HBE on body composition, physical function, cardiometabolic health, and HRQoL. The pooled results showed that HBE significantly reduced BMI and significantly improved HRQoL. These findings suggest that HBE may reduce body mass index and improve self-reported health status in postmenopausal and older women.
However, the pooled effects of HBE on physical function (TUGT, 5 × STS, handgrip strength and 6MWT) and on cardiometabolic markers (triglycerides and blood pressure) did not reach statistical significance, and the effect on body fat percentage did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.06). Overall, the current evidence provides stronger support for a role of HBE in reducing BMI and improving HRQoL than for improving measured physical function or cardiometabolic markers. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because several outcomes were based on a limited number of trials and showed substantial between-study heterogeneity.

Potential pathways through which HBE could influence functional outcomes include improvements in muscle strength, neuromuscular control, and habitual physical activity. After menopause, declining estrogen levels may impair skeletal muscle protein homeostasis, muscle-bone interactions, and lower-limb strength, thereby contributing to reduced physical function and increased vulnerability to functional decline. Even when home-based training is performed at relatively low to moderate intensity, repeated resistance exercises, walking activities, balance tasks, and sit-to-stand movements may provide sufficient stimulus to promote muscular and neuromuscular adaptation.
These adaptations may improve lower-limb strength, postural control, and movement efficiency. Walking-based or aerobic components of HBE may also improve gait economy and cardiorespiratory efficiency, which could contribute to walking capacity, although the pooled effect on the 6MWT did not reach statistical significance in the present analysis.

If functional effects are present, they may reflect the combined influence of improved muscle strength, better postural regulation, enhanced walking capacity, and increased engagement in daily physical activity.
This meta-analysis found that HBE significantly reduced BMI, whereas its effect on BFP was not statistically significant. This finding requires careful interpretation. BMI is an indirect and composite indicator that reflects total body mass relative to height, but it does not distinguish between fat mass, lean mass, and fluid status. If HBE reduces fat mass while maintaining or increasing lean tissue, BMI may decrease without a clear corresponding reduction in BFP. In addition, only four trials reported BFP, the confidence interval was wide and crossed the null, and differences in measurement methods may have reduced statistical power and increased uncertainty.

The magnitude of these effects also needs to be weighed against clinical relevance. The pooled reduction in BMI (0.57 kg/m^2) is smaller than the minimal important difference of 1.0 kg/m^2 used in the GRADE assessment, and BMI cannot distinguish a loss of fat mass from a loss of lean tissue. The reductions in body fat percentage (0.31%), TUGT time (0.64 s), handgrip strength (1.43 kg) and triglycerides (8.96 mg/dL) were likewise each smaller than their respective minimal important differences, whereas the reduction in 5 × STS time (1.92 s) exceeded its minimal important difference of 1.5 s but had a confidence interval that crossed the null (Supplementary Table S3). The statistically significant reduction in BMI should therefore not be read as a demonstrated clinical benefit.
Previous evidence suggests that exercise training can improve body composition in postmenopausal women, with aerobic training being more closely associated with fat loss and resistance training contributing to muscle maintenance or gain.

The present findings are therefore consistent with the view that HBE may support weight-related outcomes, but they also indicate that current evidence is insufficient to confirm a robust effect on BFP.
In terms of physical function, the direction of the pooled estimates was consistent across TUGT, 5 × STS, handgrip strength and 6MWT, although none reached statistical significance and the prediction intervals crossed the null for the most heterogeneous outcomes. TUGT and 5 × STS mainly reflect lower-limb strength, balance control, transfer ability, and functional mobility. Handgrip strength is widely used as an indicator of overall muscle function, whereas 6MWT reflects walking endurance and integrated functional capacity. Taken together, these estimates are too imprecise to establish an effect on measured physical function, and should not be read as evidence of benefit.

HBE did not show statistically significant effects on triglycerides, SBP, or DBP. Several explanations are possible. First, only a small number of studies contributed data to these outcomes, limiting statistical power. Second, the intensity and duration of many home-based programs may have been insufficient to produce marked cardiometabolic adaptations. Third, some participants may have had relatively low baseline cardiometabolic risk, leaving limited room for improvement. Fourth, blood pressure and lipid outcomes may also be influenced by diet, medication use, baseline disease status, and daily lifestyle factors that were not fully controlled in the original trials. This pattern is consistent with a recent meta-analysis of rehabilitation in postmenopausal women, which likewise found no significant pooled effect on blood pressure or on objectively measured physical performance. Compared with supervised exercise, HBE often emphasizes safety and long-term adherence, and the actual training intensity may therefore be insufficient to induce strong cardiometabolic adaptation.

The pooled effect on HRQoL was statistically significant (SMD = 0.51; 95% CI: 0.08 to 0.94; p = 0.025), but the prediction interval crossed the null and the estimate lost significance in two of the prespecified sensitivity analyses (restriction to trials with documented menopausal status and exclusion of all grade C trials). The direction and magnitude are consistent with a recent meta-analysis of exercise and mind–body exercise across the menopausal transition, which reported a large pooled improvement in HRQoL. Interpretation is also complicated by differences in clinical background, inconsistency in measurement instruments, and the multidimensional nature of HRQoL. HRQoL is influenced not only by physical function but also by pain, sleep, psychological status, chronic disease burden, and social support. Different instruments may emphasize different domains, thereby increasing between-study heterogeneity. The certainty of this evidence was rated very low on GRADE, and the effect of HBE on HRQoL in postmenopausal and older women should therefore be regarded as uncertain pending further confirmation.

HBE has practical value for postmenopausal and older women who have difficulty participating in facility-based exercise over the long term. For women with travel limitations, financial constraints, limited time, or chronic disease management needs, HBE can serve as an important strategy to promote physical activity. In practical prescription design, aerobic exercise, resistance training, balance exercises and flexibility training may reasonably be combined. It should be noted, however, that the present analysis did not demonstrate statistically significant effects on measured muscle strength, lower-limb function or walking capacity; the recommendation to combine modalities rests on the content of the included programs and on general physical activity guidance rather than on the pooled estimates reported here.

Individualization and safety should be emphasized when HBE is implemented. For women with chronic diseases, osteoporosis, poor physical function, or limited exercise experience, exercise intensity and progression should be adjusted according to health status and baseline fitness. Video instruction, mobile applications, elastic-band training, exercise logs, and home monitoring tools may help improve adherence and training quality. When necessary, remote supervision or periodic evaluation can be used to ensure safety. From this perspective, HBE is not only an alternative exercise format but also a potentially important component of long-term health management and functional maintenance in postmenopausal and older women. For such programs to be reproducible and clinically interpretable, future trials should report exercise prescription using a standardized framework such as the Consensus on Exercise Reporting Template (CERT), so that the delivered dose, progression and supervision can be compared across studies; this issue is discussed further in Section 4.6.

This review has several limitations. First, some outcomes were based on a small number of studies, particularly blood pressure, triglycerides, BFP, and 6MWT, which limits the stability of the effect estimates. Second, the included studies differed in exercise modality, training frequency, intervention duration, supervision format, and participant comorbidity profile, which may have contributed to clinical heterogeneity. Third, the original trials provided limited objective reporting of HBE adherence, actual exercise dose, and achieved training intensity, which restricted interpretation of dose–response relationships. Fourth, some studies had incomplete reporting of randomization procedures, inadequate allocation concealment, difficulties with blinding, or potential outcome-measurement bias, which may affect certainty of evidence. Fifth, only English-language studies were included, so language bias cannot be completely excluded. Sixth, because most outcomes included few studies, the ability to assess publication bias was limited.

In addition, RoB 2 was applied at the trial level rather than separately for each specific outcome, which may obscure outcome-specific differences in risk of bias, particularly between objective physical-performance outcomes and self-reported HRQoL. Seventh, the registered protocol specified postmenopausal women and excluded women whose menopausal status was not documented, whereas seven trials that enrolled older women without a stated menopause criterion (grade C) were retained, which is a protocol deviation. The search term covering this branch was nested within the menopausal concept and was not developed as a separate search concept, so these trials were not systematically identified and the review should not be read as a complete synthesis of exercise trials in older women irrespective of menopausal status. This deviation has a direct bearing on the results: restricting the analysis to trials with documented menopausal status reduced the HRQoL estimate below statistical significance (SMD = 0.31; 95% CI: −0.05 to 0.66), and the HRQoL finding is reported as preliminary for this reason.

Finally, on the GRADE domains of risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, the certainty of the evidence was moderate for BMI and very low for HRQoL, and low to very low for the remaining outcomes; the conclusions should be read with this in mind.
The difficulty of characterizing the exercise actually delivered is not specific to this review. A recent systematic review of high-intensity resistance and impact training in menopausal women used the Consensus on Exercise Reporting Template (CERT) to appraise 39 trials involving 3,349 women, and reported overall completeness of intervention reporting to be moderate to good (mean 14.3 of 19 items), while items relating to progression, individualization, behavioral support and home-based delivery were frequently omitted.

Those are precisely the elements on which the present synthesis was least able to draw: progression was not reported, or was explicitly absent, in 6 of the 19 trials; supervision had to be reconstructed from brief descriptions of contact rather than taken from a stated protocol; and adherence was expressed in incompatible ways (session counts, percentages, diary data, or not at all), so that it could not be pooled. The consequence is direct. The inability to characterize the exercise actually delivered is a principal reason why dose–response questions could not be addressed here, and why between-study heterogeneity remained substantial for several outcomes. Routine use of a reporting template such as CERT, alongside explicit specification of what proportion of sessions is delivered at home, would make future syntheses of home-based exercise considerably more informative.

Future research should use larger samples and more rigorous randomized controlled designs to improve evidence quality. Investigators should further standardize HBE prescriptions by clearly reporting exercise type, intensity, frequency, session duration, total intervention duration, and supervision format. Future studies should also strengthen adherence monitoring and adverse-event reporting and should extend follow-up periods to evaluate the durability of intervention effects. For cardiometabolic and HRQoL outcomes, future trials should include adequate sample sizes and use consistent measurement tools where possible. With the development of telemedicine and digital health technology, the roles of video guidance, mobile applications, and wearable devices in HBE management also warrant further investigation.

Home-based exercise may reduce BMI and improve HRQoL in postmenopausal and older women. The evidence for effects on physical function (TUGT, 5 × STS, handgrip strength, 6MWT) and on cardiometabolic markers (triglycerides, blood pressure) remains inconclusive, with prediction intervals crossing the null for the most heterogeneous outcomes. The certainty of the evidence was moderate for BMI and very low for HRQoL. Before clinical recommendations can be made, further high-quality randomized controlled trials with standardized exercise prescriptions, longer follow-up, and routine reporting of adherence and adverse events are needed.

Objective: To assess the impact of exercise on bone metabolism in postmenopausal women through meta-analysis, and to offer evidence-based guidance for preventing and managing osteoporosis in this population.
Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, and other databases using keywords such as “exercise,” “postmenopausal women,” and “bone metabolism” to identify randomized controlled trials published up to 2024 on the effect of exercise on bone metabolism in postmenopausal women. Studies were selected according to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were analyzed using Review Manager 5.4 and Stata17. Study quality was assessed with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool. Effect sizes were pooled as standardized mean differences(SMDs)with 95% confidence intervals(CIs), and heterogeneity was evaluated with the I²statistic. A fixed-effects model was used when I²≤50%; otherwise, a random-effects model was applied. The overall evidence certainty was rated using the Grading of recommendations assessment, development, and evaluation(GRADE)system.

Results: A meta-analysis of 24 studies(1067 subjects total)showed that exercise significantly elevated the levels of alkaline phosphatase(ALP)(SMD = 0.49, 95%CI: 0.21-0.77, P = 0.0006), N-terminal propeptide of type I procollagen(P1NP)(SMD = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.24 to 1.01, P = 0.002)and osteocalcin(OC)(SMD = 0.21, 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.37, P = 0.01); exercise significantly reduced the levels of parathyroid hormone(PTH)(SMD=-0.51, 95% CI: -0.77 to -0.25, P = 0.0001)and type I collagen cross-linked C-terminal peptide(CTX)(SMD=-0.32, 95% CI: -0.51to-0.12, P = 0.001). Subgroup analyses showed that aerobic exercise(SMD=-0.35, 95% CI: -0.65 to -0.06, P = 0.02) significantly reduced CTX levels, while both aerobic exercise(SMD = 0.23, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.44, P = 0.04)and resistance exercise(SMD = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.10 to 1.20, P = 0.02)significantly increased OC levels.

Exercise interventions lasting ≤6 months(SMD=-0.45, 95% CI: -0.72 to -0.18, P = 0.001)and sessions of ≤60 min(SMD=-0.48, 95% CI: -0.80 to -0.17, P = 0.003)both significantly reduced CTX levels, exercise interventions lasting ≤6 months(SMD = 0.35, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.57, P = 0.002)and sessions of ≤60 min(SMD = 0.20, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.39, P = 0.04)can significantly both increase OC levels.
Conclusion: Exercise significantly improves bone metabolism in postmenopausal women by reducing bone resorption and promoting bone formation. Aerobic exercise lowers CTX levels, while both aerobic and resistance exercise increase OC levels. Short-term (≤6 months) and moderate-length (≤60 minutes/session) interventions are particularly effective. However, more high-quality randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these benefits.
Systematic review registration: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/, identifier CRD42024610810.

The initial screening identified 1653 articles, including 331 articles in PubMed database, 365 articles in Embase database, 278 articles in Cochrane Library database, 225 articles in Web of Science database, 178 articles in Scopus database, and 276 articles in Google Scholar database. We obtained 835 articles by de-weighting with EndNote 20 software, excluded 751 articles after reading the titles and abstracts, excluded 7 articles with low relevance, and read through the full text of the remaining 84 articles to assess whether to include them. Among them, 13 interventions did not match the target group, 9 controls did not meet the criteria, 15 interventions did not meet the inclusion criteria, 12 outcome indicators did not match, 7 had no control, and 4 were unable to extract data, and finally, the remaining 24 papers were included in the Meta-analysis. (Figure 1).

Figure 1. PRISMA study flow diagram.
Nine studies reported the method of random sequence generation (computer-generated random numbers, variable block randomization, stratified randomization, coin tossing, urn design). One study provided information on allocation concealment, stating that sealed opaque envelopes were used. Twenty-two studies reported the number of dropouts and losses to follow-up. Four studies conducted an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis, while seventeen performed a per-protocol (PP) analysis; four did not specify whether ITT or PP was applied. Four studies reported a trial registration number. In summary, since blinding is difficult to implement in exercise intervention studies, most studies were judged to be at “high risk” of bias. The results of the risk of bias assessment are shown in Figures 2 and 3.

The results showed that serum phosphorus (SMD = 0.10, 95% CI: -0.18 to 0.39, P = 0.48) tended to increase in the exercise group compared to the control group but was not significant. (Figure 4).

There were 7 RCTs on the effect of exercise on CTX in postmenopausal women. Meta-analysis showed moderate heterogeneity of the included studies in the exercise group compared to the control group (I^2 = 35%, P = 0.12), so a fixed-effects model was used (Figures 10 - 12). The results showed that the CTX levels in the exercise group were significantly lower than those in the control group (SMD = -0.32, 95% CI: -0.51 to -0.12, P = 0.001).

The results of the subgroup analysis by exercise type showed that aerobic exercise (SMD = -0.35, 95% CI: -0.65 to -0.06, P = 0.02) significantly reduced CTX levels; resistance exercise (SMD = -0.32, 95% CI: -1.10 to 0.47, P = 0.43), combined aerobic plus resistance exercise (SMD = -0.34, 95% CI: -0.74 to 0.06, P = 0.10) and Tai Chi (SMD = -0.24, 95% CI: -0.63 to 0.15, P = 0.23) showed a trend toward reducing CTX, but without statistical significance (Figure 10). The further stratification of sample size may have resulted in smaller pooled effect sizes and an insufficient number of studies, leading to unstable statistical results and less convincing findings. The results of cycle subgroup analysis showed that exercise for ≤6 months (SMD=-0.45, 95% CI: -0.72 to -0.18, P = 0.001) significantly reduced CTX levels; exercise for >6 months (SMD=-0.17, 95% CI: 0.46 to 0.11, P = 0.22) had a trend to reduce CTX levels and was not significant (Figure 11).

Subgroup analysis of the duration of a single exercise session showed that exercise of ≤60 min (SMD=-0.48, 95% CI: -0.80 to -0.17, P = 0.003) significantly reduced CTX levels, and exercise of >60 min (SMD=-0.22, 95% CI: -0.47 to 0.03, P = 0.09) had a trend to reduce CTX levels and was not significant (Figure 12).

There were 11 RCTs on the effect of exercise on OC in postmenopausal women. Meta-analysis showed moderate heterogeneity of the included studies in the exercise group compared to the control group (I^2 = 14%, P = 0.29), so a fixed-effects model was used (Figures 13 - 15). The results showed a trend of increasing OC in the exercise group compared to the control group (SMD = 0.21, 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.37, P = 0.01) and were not significant.

The subgroup analysis by exercise type showed that aerobic exercise (SMD = 0.23, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.44, P = 0.04) and resistance exercise significantly (SMD = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.10 to 1.20, P = 0.02) increased OC levels; impact exercise (SMD = 0.34, 95% CI: -0.17 to 0.85, P = 0.19), combined aerobic plus resistance exercise (SMD = 0.23, 95% CI: -0.50 to 0.96, P = 0.54), Tai Chi (SMD = -0.03, 95% CI: -0.42 to 0.35, P = 0.86) and whole body vibration training (SMD = -0.09, 95% CI: -0.69 to 0.51, P = 0.77) showed a trend toward reducing OC, but without statistical significance (Figure 13). The refinement of sample size classification may have resulted in a smaller pooled effect size, and the insufficient number of studies led to unstable statistical results, making the findings less convincing. Cycle time subgroup analysis showed that exercise ≤6 months (SMD = 0.35, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.57, P = 0.002) significantly elevated OC. exercise >6 months (SMD = 0.06, 95% CI: -0.17 to 0.28, P = 0.62) showed a trend toward increasing OC levels and was not significant (Figure 14).

Subgroup analysis of the duration of a single exercise session showed that exercise for ≤60 min (SMD = 0.20, 95% CI: 0.01 to 0.39, P = 0.04) elevated OC content; exercise for >60 min (SMD=-0.22, 95% CI: -0.07, 0.50, P = 0.13) tended to decrease OC content and was non-significant (Figure 15). 11 studies reported the effect of exercise on OC in postmenopausal women, so we assessed their publication bias. The funnel plot (Supplementary Figure S1) and Egger’s test (P = 0.953) (Table 3) showed no evidence of publication bias.
